Marine biologists returned to the fjord last month after a three-year absence, and what they found surprised them. The colony of blue mussels that once coated the eastern rocks had thinned to a few scattered patches, and the kelp forest that sheltered juvenile cod had retreated to deeper water. The team suspects that warmer summers have shifted the plankton bloom earlier in the season, leaving newly settled larvae with less to eat.

Working from a converted fishing trawler, the researchers lowered a remotely operated vehicle to survey the seabed at twelve fixed stations. The vehicle carried cameras and a small claw for sampling sediment, and it logged temperature, salinity and oxygen at every stop. On the third day the weather turned, and the crew spent two nights anchored in a sheltered cove while the swell rolled past the headland.

Divers also collected short sediment cores at six of the stations, pushing clear plastic tubes into the mud and capping them by hand. Back in the laboratory the cores will be sliced at one-centimetre intervals and dated with lead-210, which should show when the mussel shells stopped accumulating. A first look at the slices suggests the change was gradual rather than sudden.

Local fishers have watched the same shift with unease. Several said the cod they catch now are smaller and thinner than the ones their fathers landed, and that the mussel beds were already patchy before the survey began. A handful of the older fishers disagreed, arguing that the beds have always varied from year to year and that the survey simply arrived in a poor season. The research team plans to interview a dozen of them and to combine those accounts with the survey data, on the hunch that the two lines of evidence will point to the same set of pressures.

Under the ministry's annual monitoring programme, the results must be filed by December, and the funding for the next three seasons depends on that report. The team has promised to publish the raw station data alongside the report so that independent groups can repeat the analysis.
